site.name: Grant C Anthony
site.about:
I have been taking photographs, on and off, for close to thirty years. It started with my father-in-law, whose influence got me going.

My wife is also a keen photographer, and an exceptionally good one. We travel together in our camper van, and on city breaks and photography holidays.

What I go out for is the experience: being in the moment, in the flow, where time gets lost. I keep my editing light. That side is my wife's passion more than mine.

In my bag: a Canon EOS R5 with 16-35, 24-70, 70-200 and 100-400 zooms, and a nifty fifty. Kase filters. A Three Legged Thing Winston and Corey, a Peak Design carbon-fibre tripod for cities, and a Leica D-Lux 8: truly pocket-sized, with a brilliant monochrome mode, which makes it great for street.
site.learnIntro: What I have learned in close to thirty years behind a camera, about light, composition and the craft.

glossary.def: A doubling or halving of the light. One stop brighter lets in twice as much light; one stop darker lets in half.
The adjustable opening in the lens. It controls how much light gets in and how much of the scene is sharp.
How aperture is written, such as f/2.8 or f/16. A smaller number means a bigger opening and more light.
How long the sensor is exposed to light, such as 1/250 s or 2 s. Fast speeds freeze motion; slow ones blur it.
How much the camera amplifies the signal from the sensor. Higher ISO brightens the image but adds grain.
How much of the scene, front to back, looks acceptably sharp. Smaller apertures and greater distance give more.
The lens setting in millimetres. Shorter (such as 16 mm) takes in a wide view; longer (such as 400 mm) magnifies a small part of it.
Neutral density filter. Dark glass that cuts the light evenly without changing its colour, so you can use slower shutter speeds.
A filter you rotate to cut reflected glare. It deepens blue skies and removes shine from water and wet leaves.
A filter that is dark at one end and clear at the other, used to hold back a bright sky.
A file holding everything the sensor recorded, without the camera's processing. It looks flat but gives the most room to edit.
The setting that makes white look white under different light, from warm tungsten to cool shade.
Taking several frames of the same scene at different exposures, to choose from or blend later.
Softening of the whole image at very small apertures, usually noticeable beyond about f/16.
Roughly the hour after sunrise and before sunset, when low sun gives warm, soft, directional light.
The time when the sun is just below the horizon, before sunrise or after sunset, and the sky turns deep blue.
Taking several frames focused at different distances and blending them so the whole subject is sharp.
The way distant objects look closer together in a telephoto photograph. It comes from standing far away, not from the lens itself.
The empty area around a subject. It gives the subject room and sets the mood.
The way parallel vertical lines appear to lean together when the camera is tilted up at a building.
A system in the lens or camera that reduces blur from hand shake. Turn it off on a tripod.
A lens that can shift the image up or down without tilting the camera, keeping verticals straight.

lessons.title: The exposure triangle
lessons.summary: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO decide how bright a photograph is, and each one changes how it looks. Move the controls and see for yourself.
lessons.body:
Every exposure comes down to three settings. Each one lets in more or less light, and each one has a side effect you can see in the picture.

[[exposure]]

## Aperture

The aperture is the opening in the lens, written as an f-number. **A smaller number means a bigger opening**, so f/2.8 lets in far more light than f/16.

It also controls depth of field. Wide open, only your subject is sharp and the background melts away. Stopped down to f/11 or f/16, everything from the foreground rocks to the far hills stays sharp, which is why most landscape work sits there.

## Shutter speed

How long the sensor is exposed. 1/1000 s freezes a wave mid-break. A full second turns moving water into mist.

The catch is camera shake. A rough rule for handheld shooting: keep the shutter at least as fast as one over your focal length, so 1/50 s on a 50 mm lens. Any slower and you need a tripod.

## ISO

How strongly the camera amplifies the signal. Doubling the ISO brightens the image by one stop, but adds grain and loses detail in the shadows. Keep it as low as the light allows.

## Stops

The three are linked by **stops**. One stop is a doubling or halving of the light. Going from f/8 to f/5.6, from 1/125 s to 1/60 s, or from ISO 400 to 800 each adds one stop.

> Change one setting by a stop and you can balance it by moving another the opposite way.

That trade is the whole game. f/8 at 1/125 s and f/5.6 at 1/250 s give the same brightness. The difference is what you want sharp and what you want frozen.

## My one tip

Don't be afraid of manual mode. Out in the field, there is no better way to learn how the exposure triangle works. Every change you make, you see straight away.
lessons.challenge: Put the camera in manual. Photograph the same scene at f/4, f/8 and f/16, adjusting the shutter speed each time to keep the brightness the same. Compare what is sharp in each.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Which aperture lets in the most light?
* f/2.8
- f/8
- f/16

Q: You move from 1/125 s to 1/250 s. How do you keep the same brightness using the aperture?
* Open up one stop, for example from f/8 to f/5.6
- Close down one stop, for example from f/8 to f/11
- Leave the aperture alone and nothing changes

Q: What is the side effect of raising the ISO?
* More grain and less shadow detail
- A shallower depth of field
- More motion blur

lessons.title: Reading the light
lessons.summary: The same hill looks completely different at seven in the morning and two in the afternoon. Learn to see the light before you look for a subject.
lessons.body:
Good landscape photographs are mostly about light. The subject matters less than you think: the same view can be flat at noon and extraordinary an hour after sunrise.

The light is also why I go out at all. Watching it build and change is when I lose track of time completely, and for me that is half the point of photography.

## Golden hour

The hour after sunrise and the hour before sunset. The sun is low, so light comes in from the side, warm and soft, and every ridge and wall throws a long shadow. Texture appears that simply is not there at midday.

The further north you go, the more the timing swings with the seasons. In midsummer the golden light can last for hours. In midwinter the whole short day can feel like golden hour.

## Blue hour

The time just after sunset and just before sunrise, when the sun is below the horizon. The sky turns deep blue, street lights and windows come on, and towns look their best. Bring a tripod, because exposures run to several seconds.

[[photo:ericusspitze-blue-hour]]

## Overcast

Cloud works like a huge softbox. Shadows vanish and colours deepen, which suits woodland, waterfalls and close detail. When the sky is a flat white lid, leave it out of the frame.

## Weather is the light

Some of the best light arrives either side of rain. A break in the cloud after a squall can spotlight one hillside while everything around it stays dark.

- Look for clearing showers in the forecast, not clear skies
- Arrive early and be prepared to wait
- Keep shooting as the weather moves through

> Bad weather makes good photographs. Bad light does not.
lessons.challenge: Pick one view near home. Photograph it at sunrise, at midday and at sunset on the same day, from the same spot, and compare.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does golden hour bring out texture?
* The low sun lights the scene from the side and casts long shadows
- The light is brighter than at midday
- The sky is completely clear

Q: Which subjects suit an overcast day?
* Woodland, waterfalls and close detail
- Wide views with a big empty sky
- Silhouettes against the sun

Q: What kind of forecast is most promising for dramatic light?
* Clearing showers
- Clear skies all day
- Steady rain all day

lessons.title: Night and blue hour in cities
lessons.summary: Cities come alive after sunset. For a short time the sky and the street lights balance perfectly, and that window is worth planning around.
lessons.body:
Cities change after the sun goes down. Lit windows, glowing signs and a deep blue sky make even ordinary buildings look special.

## Blue hour is the window

About twenty to forty minutes after sunset, depending on the season and how far north you are, the sky fades to deep blue while street and window lights come on. For a while the two are close in brightness, so one exposure holds detail in both. Later, the sky turns black and the lights burn out.

[[guide:planner]]

[[photo:Der Spiegel]]

## Settings

- Tripod, lowest ISO, f/8 to f/11, and let the shutter run for as long as it needs
- Shoot in RAW and set the white balance afterwards. Mixed street lighting confuses the camera
- Bracket your exposures. City scenes at night often have more range than one frame can hold
- At small apertures, bright lights turn into star shapes

## Movement

Anything moving during a long exposure turns into a streak. Traffic becomes ribbons of red and white light, and people walking past disappear or leave ghosts.

## Practical points

- Get there before sunset to find your spot and compose while you can still see
- Reflections in water and wet streets double the light, so rain is not always bad news
- Check whether tripods are allowed. Many bridges, viewing platforms and private squares do not permit them
- Keep your kit close and stay aware of your surroundings

> Arrive in daylight. Leave in the dark.
lessons.challenge: Pick one city view. Photograph it every ten minutes from sunset until the sky is black, then compare which frame has the best balance.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why is blue hour so good for city photographs?
* The sky and the artificial lights are close in brightness
- The street lights are switched off
- The sky is completely black

Q: Why set white balance afterwards, from a RAW file?
* Mixed street lighting confuses the camera's automatic setting
- RAW files have no colour
- White balance cannot be set in the camera

Q: What happens to traffic during a 20-second exposure?
* It turns into streaks of light
- It freezes sharply
- It makes the image darker

lessons.title: Planning a photography trip
lessons.summary: Good light is mostly luck, but you can tip the odds. Time, weather and a bit of homework put you in the right place when it happens.
lessons.body:
We travel in our camper van and go on city breaks and photography holidays. Wherever you go, good photographs come from being in the right place at the right time, and that is something you can plan for.

## Know when the light happens

Golden hour and blue hour times change every day and with every place. Check them before you go.

[[guide:planner]]

## Scout first

- Look at the place on a map and in other people's photographs, to see what is there and where the light falls
- Note which way the main view faces. East-facing scenes suit sunrise; west-facing scenes suit sunset
- Visit in the middle of the day if you can, when the light is poor, to find your spot without pressure

## Watch the weather, not just the forecast icon

- Clearing showers and broken cloud give better light than a clear blue sky
- Still, cold mornings bring mist and reflections
- Wind matters as much as rain: it ruins reflections and shakes tripods
- Tide times matter on the coast

## Pack for the conditions

- Spare batteries, especially in the cold
- A head torch for early starts and late finishes
- Something to sit on and something warm. Good light often means waiting

## Leave room for luck

A plan gets you there. What you find when you arrive is often better. Keep the camera out on the walk back.

[[photo:Botallack]]

> Plan for the light. Stay open to everything else.
lessons.challenge: Use the planner to find tomorrow's golden hour for a place within an hour of home. Go, arrive twenty minutes early, and stay until it ends.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Which kind of weather usually gives the most interesting light?
* Broken cloud and clearing showers
- A clear blue sky all day
- Thick, flat cloud

Q: A view faces west. When is it likely to be at its best?
* Around sunset
- Around sunrise
- At midday

Q: Why visit a location in the middle of the day?
* To find your spot without the pressure of the light changing
- Because midday light is best
- Because there are fewer people at night

lessons.title: The rule of thirds
lessons.summary: Split the frame into nine and put what matters where the lines cross. The simplest way to stop every picture looking like a snapshot.
lessons.body:
Most beginners put the subject in the middle of the frame. It is the obvious place, and it is usually the dullest. The rule of thirds is the quickest fix.

[[guide:thirds]]

## How it works

Imagine two lines across the frame and two lines down it, splitting it into nine equal parts. Place your subject on one of the four points where the lines cross, and run strong edges such as the horizon along one of the lines.

An off-centre subject creates tension. The eye has somewhere to go, and the empty part of the frame starts to matter.

## Use the grid in your camera

Almost every camera and phone can show a thirds grid on screen. Turn it on and leave it on. After a few weeks you will place things on the thirds without thinking.

## Give it room

If your subject is looking or moving, put the space in front of it, not behind. A walker heading left belongs on the right third, with the empty frame ahead of them.

## When to break it

- Symmetry and reflections usually want the centre
- A single small subject in a big empty space can sit almost anywhere
- Square frames often suit a central subject

> The rule of thirds is a starting point, not a law. Learn it well enough that breaking it is a choice.
lessons.challenge: Turn on the grid in your camera or phone and leave it on for a week. Take every photograph with the main subject on one of the four crossing points.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Where does the rule of thirds suggest you place the subject?
* On one of the four points where the grid lines cross
- Exactly in the centre
- In a corner of the frame

Q: A walker is heading left. Where should they go?
* On the right third, with space ahead of them
- On the left third, close to the edge they are walking towards
- In the centre

Q: Which kind of scene usually suits a centred subject instead?
* A symmetrical reflection
- A lone walker on a beach
- A tree on a hillside

lessons.title: Where to put the horizon
lessons.summary: High, low or dead centre. Where the horizon sits decides whether a photograph is about the land or the sky.
lessons.body:
The horizon is usually the strongest line in a landscape. Where you put it tells the viewer what the photograph is about before they have looked at anything else.

[[guide:horizon]]

## Low horizon: sky-led

Put the horizon on the lower third when the sky is doing something worth showing: storm cloud, a sunset, a big clearing after rain. The land becomes a thin base for the drama above it.

## High horizon: land-led

Put it on the upper third when the interest is in front of you: rocks on the shore, patterns in the sand, a path leading in. On a flat grey day this is often the only way to make a landscape work, because it leaves the dull sky out.

## Centred: for reflections

A horizon through the middle splits the frame in two equal halves. That usually feels static, which is exactly why it suits a mirror-calm loch. The reflection and the scene balance each other.

## Keep it level

A sloping horizon is the most common mistake in landscape photography, and the easiest to fix. Turn on the level in your camera, or straighten it afterwards. On the coast, a tilted sea looks as if it is draining out of the picture.

> Decide what the photograph is about, then give it the most room.
lessons.challenge: Find one open view and take three photographs: horizon on the lower third, on the upper third and through the middle. Decide which tells the story best.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The sky is full of storm cloud. Where do you put the horizon?
* On the lower third
- On the upper third
- Out of the frame entirely

Q: When does a centred horizon work well?
* With a mirror-calm reflection
- With a dull grey sky
- With an interesting foreground and a plain sky

Q: What is the most common horizon mistake?
* A horizon that slopes
- A horizon on the lower third
- A horizon on the upper third

lessons.title: Leading lines
lessons.summary: Roads, walls, rivers and shorelines can walk the eye straight to your subject. Find the line first, then the point it leads to.
lessons.body:
The eye follows lines. Put a line in the frame that runs towards your subject and you have done half the work of telling people where to look.

[[guide:lines]]

## Where to find them

- Roads and paths running away from you
- Dry stone walls and fences crossing a hillside
- Rivers, burns and the curve of a shoreline
- Piers, railings and rows of windows in town

## Make them lead somewhere

A line that runs out of the side of the frame takes the eye with it. The strongest lines start near a corner or the bottom edge and end at something worth looking at: a building, a peak, a figure.

## Get low and go wide

A wide-angle lens close to the ground stretches lines out and makes them converge faster. A wall that looks ordinary at head height can sweep right through the frame from knee height.

## Curves

Straight lines are direct and strong. Curves, like an S-bend in a river or a road winding through a glen, slow the eye down and make it wander. Both work. Choose the one that matches the mood.

> Find the line first. Then walk until it points where you want.
lessons.challenge: Find a path, wall or shoreline. Photograph it from head height, then from knee height with your widest lens, and compare how strongly it pulls you in.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Where does a leading line usually work best?
* Starting near a corner or the bottom edge and ending at the subject
- Running out of the side of the frame
- Running straight across the middle

Q: What does getting low with a wide lens do to a line?
* Stretches it out and makes it converge faster
- Flattens it
- Makes it disappear

Q: How do curves differ from straight lines?
* They slow the eye down and make it wander
- They always look stronger
- They only work in black and white

lessons.title: Framing within the frame
lessons.summary: An archway, a window or a gap in the trees puts a border inside your photograph and holds the eye on what matters.
lessons.body:
A natural frame is anything in the scene that surrounds your subject: a doorway, branches, a window, the gap between two buildings. It adds depth, gives context and keeps the eye from drifting off the edges.

[[guide:frame]]

## Why it works

The frame creates layers. Something close, the subject further away, and the space between them make a flat image feel three-dimensional. It also shows where you were standing, which tells a story of its own.

## Keep the frame quiet

The frame should support the subject, not compete with it. It works best when it is darker than the view, or simpler. A shadowy archway around a bright street is the classic example.

## Focus and depth

Decide what should be sharp. At f/11 or f/16 both the frame and the view stay crisp. At f/2.8 the frame melts into a soft border and the subject stands out. Both are valid choices.

## Where to look

- Doorways and arches in old towns and castles
- Overhanging branches at the edge of a wood
- Rock arches and caves on the coast
- Bridges, seen from underneath

> A frame does not have to be complete. Two branches can be enough.
lessons.challenge: Find an archway, window or gap in the trees. Photograph the view through it once at f/2.8 and once at f/11, and see how the frame changes.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What makes a natural frame work best?
* Being darker or simpler than the view through it
- Being brighter than the subject
- Being as detailed as possible

Q: At f/2.8, what happens to a frame close to the lens?
* It turns into a soft border
- It becomes sharper than the subject
- Nothing, the aperture has no effect

Q: Does a frame need to go all the way round the subject?
* No, two branches can be enough
- Yes, or it does not count as a frame
- Only in portrait format

lessons.title: Symmetry and patterns
lessons.summary: Reflections, repeating shapes and perfect balance. When to centre everything, and why breaking a pattern is often the photograph.
lessons.body:
Most composition advice tells you to move the subject off-centre. Symmetry is the exception. When a scene is balanced, centring it is the strongest choice.

[[guide:symmetry]]

## Reflections

Still water is the easiest symmetry to find. Get to a loch early, before the wind gets up, put the horizon through the middle and let the reflection mirror the scene. A low angle, close to the water, makes the reflection larger.

## Built symmetry

Architecture is full of it: bridges, doorways, church interiors, corridors. Stand exactly in the middle, keep the camera level and square to the subject, and check the edges match. Being a few centimetres off-centre is very obvious in a symmetrical frame.

## Patterns

Repetition is pleasing to the eye: rows of windows, ripples in sand, stacked lobster creels on a harbour wall. Fill the frame so the pattern seems to carry on beyond the edges.

## Break the pattern

The strongest pattern photographs often contain one thing that does not fit. A single red door in a terrace. One gull on a row of posts. The pattern sets up an expectation and the break becomes the subject.

> Symmetry is calm. A broken pattern is a story.
lessons.challenge: Find a repeating pattern, such as windows, posts or boats. Photograph it so it fills the frame, then wait for or find one thing that breaks it.
lessons.quiz:
Q: How do you make a reflection look larger?
* Lower the camera, closer to the water
- Raise the camera as high as possible
- Use a longer shutter speed

Q: Why stand exactly in the middle for built symmetry?
* Being slightly off-centre is very obvious in a symmetrical frame
- It lets in more light
- It keeps the horizon level

Q: What often makes the strongest pattern photograph?
* One element that breaks the pattern
- A pattern that stops well inside the frame
- A pattern photographed from far away

lessons.title: The golden ratio
lessons.summary: The spiral and the phi grid, where they come from, and how much weight to give them.
lessons.body:
The golden ratio is about 1.618 to 1. Painters and architects have used it for centuries, and photographers borrow it as two composition guides: the golden spiral and the phi grid.

[[guide:golden]]

## The golden spiral

Divide a golden rectangle into a square and a smaller golden rectangle, then keep going. A curve drawn through the squares makes a spiral that tightens towards one point. Line up that point with your subject, and let a curve in the scene, such as a shoreline or a sweep of cloud, follow the spiral round.

The spiral can face any of four ways. Flip it to suit the photograph, not the other way round.

## The phi grid

The phi grid places its lines at about 38% and 62% of the frame, instead of the thirds at 33% and 67%. The difference is small. It pulls the subject slightly closer to the centre, which can feel calmer than a strict thirds placement.

## How much it matters

Be a little sceptical. There is not much evidence that the golden ratio looks better than other off-centre placements, and plenty of great photographs ignore it entirely. Treat it as one more way of checking a composition, and a useful one for curved subjects.

- Most editing software can show a spiral and phi grid when cropping
- Try it when cropping, not just in camera
- If it does not fit naturally, do not force it

> Guides help you see. They do not take the photograph for you.
lessons.challenge: Take five photographs you already like. Crop each with a thirds overlay and then a golden spiral or phi grid, and note which ones each guide improves.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Roughly what is the golden ratio?
* 1.618 to 1
- 1.5 to 1
- 3 to 1

Q: Where are the phi grid lines compared with the thirds?
* Slightly closer to the centre
- Further out towards the edges
- In exactly the same place

Q: How much weight should you give the golden ratio?
* Treat it as one useful way of checking a composition
- Always follow it exactly
- Ignore it completely

lessons.title: Composing a landscape
lessons.summary: A wide view rarely works on its own. Give the eye a way in, a place to rest and a reason to stay.
lessons.body:
Stand in front of a great view, take a picture, and it often looks smaller and emptier than it felt. The scene needs structure.

## Find a foreground

Get low and put something close to the lens: rocks, heather, a fence post, ripples on the shore. It gives depth and a starting point for the eye. Use a smaller aperture such as f/11 so it stays sharp along with the distance.

## Use lines

Roads, rivers, walls and shorelines lead the eye through the frame. Diagonals feel more dynamic than lines running straight across.

## Place the horizon on purpose

The rule of thirds is a useful starting point, not a law. If the sky is the story, give it two thirds of the frame. If it is a dull grey, give it a sliver or leave it out. Either way, keep the horizon level.

## Simplify

Most weak compositions have too much in them. Before you press the shutter, walk your eye round the edges of the frame and ask what each thing is doing there.

- Move a few steps to separate overlapping shapes
- Zoom in on the part of the view that drew you in
- Try a portrait frame as well as a landscape one

> If it does not add to the picture, it takes away from it.
lessons.challenge: At your next view, take one photograph as you first see it. Then get low with something close to the lens, and take a second. Compare the two.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why put something in the foreground?
* It adds depth and gives the eye a starting point
- It hides the sky
- It makes the exposure easier

Q: Which aperture keeps both a close foreground and the distance sharp?
* Around f/11
- Around f/2
- It makes no difference

Q: The sky is flat and grey. What do you do?
* Give it a sliver of the frame or leave it out
- Give it two thirds of the frame
- Put the horizon in the middle

lessons.title: Minimalism
lessons.summary: One subject, a lot of empty space and nothing else. Minimalism is the art of taking things out until the picture breaks, then putting one back.
lessons.body:
Minimalist photographs strip a scene down to as little as possible: usually one subject and a large area of empty space. Done well they are calm, strong and memorable. Done badly they are just empty.

[[guide:space]]

## Negative space

The empty area around the subject is called negative space. It is not wasted. It gives the subject room, sets the mood and makes something small feel significant. A lone boat on a flat calm sea is more powerful than the same boat in a busy harbour.

## Where to find it

- Fog and mist, which erase the background
- Flat calm water and plain skies
- Snow, sand and beaches at low tide
- Long exposures, which smooth water and cloud into plain tone
- Plain walls in towns, with one person, door or window

## Keep it simple, but not empty

The subject still needs to be placed with care. Thirds work well, and so does putting a small subject low or to one side so the space reads as deliberate. Check every edge of the frame for a stray branch, post or bird that pulls the eye away.

## Colour and tone

Limit the palette. Two or three tones, or one colour against neutral grey, works better than a full range. Many minimalist images are slightly overexposed to keep the space clean and light.

> Keep taking things out until it stops working. Then put the last one back.
lessons.challenge: Make a photograph with one subject taking up less than a tenth of the frame. Check every edge before you press the shutter.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is negative space?
* The empty area around the subject
- The dark parts of the image
- The space behind the camera

Q: Which conditions help create minimalist pictures?
* Fog, calm water and plain skies
- A busy market
- Dense woodland in bright sun

Q: How do many minimalist photographers handle exposure?
* Slightly overexpose to keep the space clean and light
- Underexpose heavily
- Always shoot at high ISO

lessons.title: Telephoto landscapes
lessons.summary: Landscapes are not only for wide-angle lenses. A long lens picks one shape out of a big view and stacks distant layers on top of each other.
lessons.body:
The usual advice for landscapes is to go wide. Some of my favourite landscape photographs come from the other end: a 100-400 mm zoom. Every Deadvlei photograph on this site was taken with it.

[[guide:focal]]

## What compression really is

People say long lenses compress a scene, making distant things look closer together. Strictly, the lens is not doing it. Perspective depends only on where you stand. A long lens lets you stand far back and still fill the frame, and from far back the near and far objects look closer in size. That is the effect you see when you move the slider.

## Why it works for landscapes

- It isolates one shape, such as a single tree, a ridge or a patch of light, from a cluttered view
- It stacks layers: hills, mist and dunes pile up into bands of tone
- It makes distant mountains and dunes loom over the foreground
- It cuts out a dull sky or an untidy edge

[[photo:Shadow line]]

Shot at 400 mm. The dune edge and the shadow become a simple graphic line because the lens cuts away everything around them.

## Practical points

- Long lenses magnify shake. Use a tripod, or keep the shutter at least as fast as one over the focal length
- Heat haze softens distant detail on hot days and over warm ground. Early morning is clearer
- Wind matters more. Shelter the tripod and hang your bag from it
- You do not always need a small aperture. With everything far away, f/8 to f/11 is usually enough for front-to-back sharpness

> Go wide to show where you were. Go long to show what you saw.
lessons.challenge: Go somewhere you would normally shoot wide. Take the longest lens you own and make three photographs that each show only one thing.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What actually causes the compressed look of a telephoto landscape?
* Standing further away from the subject
- The glass in a long lens squashing the image
- Using a small aperture

Q: Why is a tripod more important with a long lens?
* A long lens magnifies camera shake
- Long lenses let in less light
- Autofocus does not work handheld

Q: What can soften distant detail on a hot day?
* Heat haze
- Lens compression
- High ISO

lessons.title: Long exposure
lessons.summary: Leave the shutter open for seconds or minutes and the moving world disappears. Water turns to mist, clouds to streaks, traffic to ribbons of light.
lessons.body:
A long exposure records everything that happens while the shutter is open. Anything still stays sharp. Anything moving smears, fades or vanishes. That contrast is the whole effect.

[[guide:longexp]]

## ND filters

In daylight there is far too much light for a long exposure. A neutral density filter is dark glass that cuts the light without changing its colour, measured in stops.

- **3 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 1/15 s. Softens waterfalls and waves
- **6 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 1/2 s. Smooths moving water
- **10 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 8 s. Flattens the sea and streaks clouds

Every stop doubles the time. Phone apps will do the sums, but it is worth knowing them roughly in your head.

## The method

- Use a solid tripod and a remote release or the 2-second timer
- When the camera comes off the tripod, switch the timer off. Forgetting to is my longest-running mistake
- Turn off image stabilisation when the camera is on a tripod
- Compose and focus before you screw on a dark filter, then switch to manual focus
- With a DSLR, cover the viewfinder during the exposure so light does not leak in

I use Kase ND filters on a Three Legged Thing Winston. I never rely on a single frame: I take a lot of shots at a few different exposure times and choose afterwards. A few seconds either way changes how the water looks, and it is far easier to pick the right one at home than to guess on the spot.

## Water

A second or two turns waves into soft texture. Thirty seconds or more turns the sea into mist around the rocks. Keep something solid in the frame, such as rocks, a pier or a post, so the smoothness has something to contrast with.

[[photo:Lofoten shore]]

## Light trails

At night you do not need a filter. Ten to thirty seconds at f/8 to f/11 turns traffic into streams of red and white light, while the buildings stay sharp.

[[photo:Chilehaus]]

## Blue hour

After sunset the light falls fast enough that exposures of several seconds happen without any filter. Still water becomes a mirror and lit windows glow.

> Find something that will not move, then let everything else go.
lessons.challenge: Find moving water. Take the same composition at 1/125 s, 1 s and 30 s (use an ND filter if it is bright), and compare how the water changes.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What does an ND filter do?
* Cuts the light without changing its colour
- Darkens only the sky
- Removes reflections

Q: Why compose and focus before fitting a dark ND filter?
* The viewfinder and autofocus struggle with so little light
- The filter changes the focal length
- The filter has to be fitted at night

Q: Do you need a filter for light trails at night?
* No, there is little enough light already
- Yes, always a 10-stop filter
- Yes, a polariser

lessons.title: Filters
lessons.summary: Most effects can be added later in editing. Two cannot: a polariser removing glare, and an ND filter slowing the shutter. Those are the filters worth carrying.
lessons.body:
I carry Kase filters, and in practice I reach for two kinds: neutral density filters for long exposures and a polariser. Almost everything else can be done afterwards in editing. These two cannot.

## The polariser

A polariser cuts reflected glare. Turn the ring and you can watch the sky deepen, clouds stand out, the shine disappear from wet leaves and the surface of water turn clear enough to see the stones below.

[[guide:polariser]]

- It works best with the sun at right angles to the direction you are pointing
- On a wide lens it can darken one part of the sky more than another, so watch the edges
- It costs one to two stops of light
- Take it off at night and when there is nothing to remove

## ND filters

An ND filter is plain dark glass that lets you use a slow shutter speed in daylight. The Long exposure lesson covers them in detail.

- **3 stops:** softens moving water a little
- **6 stops:** turns waves into texture
- **10 stops:** flattens the sea and streaks the clouds

## Graduated filters

A grad is dark at the top and clear at the bottom, to hold back a bright sky. They are less essential than they used to be, because you can take two exposures and blend them, but they still save time in the field.

## Looking after them

- Keep them clean. A smudge shows up badly in a long exposure
- Use a lens hood or shade the filter if the sun is near the frame
- Check for colour casts on very dark ND filters and correct them afterwards

> If software can do it later, leave the filter in the bag.
lessons.challenge: Find water with the sun to your side. Take one photograph with a polariser turned for maximum effect and one with it turned for minimum, and compare them.
lessons.quiz:
Q: When does a polariser have the strongest effect on the sky?
* When the sun is at right angles to where you point the camera
- When you point the camera straight at the sun
- At night

Q: What does a 10-stop ND filter do to a 1/125 s exposure?
* Makes it about 8 seconds
- Makes it about 1/15 s
- Makes no difference to the shutter speed

Q: Why are graduated filters less essential than they used to be?
* You can blend two exposures in editing instead
- Modern cameras cannot use them
- They only work in black and white

lessons.title: Black and white
lessons.summary: Take the colour away and a photograph is only light, shadow, shape and texture. Some pictures get stronger. Some fall apart.
lessons.body:
Black and white is not colour with something missing. It is a different way of seeing, built entirely on tone: how light or dark each part of the picture is.

## When it works

- Strong light and deep shadow
- Texture: stone, bark, weathered skin, sand
- Shape and line, especially in architecture
- Street scenes where colour is cluttered or distracting
- Dull, grey days, where the colour has nothing to offer anyway

[[photo:Walk]]

On a busy street, colour pulls the eye everywhere: signs, clothes, vans. In mono only the shapes and the light are left, and the woman at the crossing becomes the subject.

## When it does not

If the picture is about colour, such as a sunset, autumn leaves or a red dress against sand, converting it throws away its reason to exist. Converting a weak photograph to black and white rarely rescues it.

## When I decide

For me it varies. Some days I go out having decided I am only shooting black and white. Sometimes I take the shot as colour and decide in the edit. And sometimes I decide on the spot, when the textures are there in front of me.

## Colour still matters

Two colours of the same brightness turn into the same grey, and the picture goes flat. Film photographers used coloured filters to control this. Digital conversions do the same thing with sliders.

[[guide:mono]]

A straight conversion of this photograph turns the sky and the dune into almost the same grey. A red filter darkens the sky and leaves the dune bright, which is why it was the classic landscape filter.

## How to work

- Shoot in colour, ideally RAW, and convert later. You keep every option
- Set the camera's picture style to monochrome if you want to see in black and white while shooting. RAW files still keep the colour
- Push the contrast more than feels comfortable, then back off a touch
- Make sure something in the frame is close to pure black and something close to pure white

My own editing is light: Lightroom, with an occasional small tweak in Photoshop. A conversion and a few contrast adjustments are usually all a black and white photograph needs from me.

[[photo:Sprinkenhof]]

> Look for light and shape. Colour can lie about a photograph; tone cannot.
lessons.challenge: Spend one walk shooting only black and white. Set the camera to monochrome so you see in tone, and keep the RAW files.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why can two different colours look flat in black and white?
* Colours of the same brightness turn into the same grey
- Black and white removes all contrast
- The camera cannot record them

Q: What does a red filter do to a blue sky in black and white?
* Darkens it
- Brightens it
- Leaves it unchanged

Q: Which subject is least likely to suit black and white?
* A sunset where the colour is the point
- Weathered stone with strong side light
- A busy street with distracting colour

lessons.title: Editing lightly
lessons.summary: Editing is not cheating, and it does not have to take hours. A few small adjustments bring a photograph back to what you saw.
lessons.body:
I keep my editing light. I use Lightroom, with an occasional small tweak in Photoshop. The aim is to bring the photograph back to what I saw, not to turn it into something it was not.

[[guide:beforeafter]]

## Why RAW files look flat

A RAW file holds everything the sensor recorded, without the camera's own processing. That gives you room to adjust, but it means the file looks dull until you do. A little contrast and colour is not exaggeration; it is finishing the job.

## A simple order of work

- **Straighten and crop.** Level the horizon first
- **White balance.** Make whites look white, or warm or cool the photograph on purpose
- **Exposure.** Set the overall brightness
- **Highlights and shadows.** Recover detail at both ends
- **Contrast and texture.** Add a little, then back off
- **Colour.** Small changes to saturation or individual colours
- **Spot removal.** Dust spots and small distractions

For buildings, the Transform tool in Lightroom straightens converging verticals. I use it only when the photograph calls for it.

## Signs you have gone too far

- Halos along the edges where sky meets land
- Skies darker than the ground in daylight
- Colours that look like no real place
- Shadows lifted until the picture looks grey

A useful habit: leave an edit overnight and look at it again before you share it.

> Edit until it looks like the moment. Then stop.
lessons.challenge: Edit one photograph using only the first five steps on the list. Then compare it with a version you have edited before and see which you prefer.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does a RAW file look flat straight from the camera?
* It has none of the camera's own processing applied
- The camera recorded it badly
- RAW files are always underexposed

Q: What is usually the first step in an edit?
* Straighten and crop
- Add saturation
- Remove dust spots

Q: Which of these is a sign of overediting?
* Halos where the sky meets the land
- A level horizon
- Accurate white balance

lessons.title: Intentional camera movement
lessons.summary: Move the camera during a long exposure on purpose and a wood becomes a painting. Easy to try, hard to master, and impossible to repeat exactly.
lessons.body:
Intentional camera movement, or ICM, breaks the first rule of photography: keep the camera still. Instead you move it deliberately while the shutter is open, turning a scene into streaks and washes of colour.

[[guide:icm]]

## The settings

Start around 1/4 s to 1/2 s. In daylight that is a long exposure, so you will need a small aperture such as f/16, the lowest ISO, and often a neutral density filter to cut the light further. Shutter priority mode makes it easy to set the speed and let the camera handle the rest.

## The movement

- **Vertical sweeps** along tree trunks are the classic. Start moving before you press the shutter and keep moving after it closes
- **Horizontal sweeps** along a horizon turn the coast into bands of sea, land and sky
- **Zoom bursts:** turn the zoom ring during the exposure for lines radiating from the centre
- **Small shakes or twists** give a softer, painterly texture

## Choose the subject carefully

ICM works best with strong, simple shapes and good colour. Lines that run in the direction of the movement stay as clean streaks; anything at an angle smears. Birch trees, autumn colour, bluebells, a sunset over the sea and city lights at night are all good starting points.

## Done for real

[[photo:cathedral-in-motion]]

A vertical sweep. The spires and tree trunks run the same way as the movement, so they hold their shape while the leaves and sky dissolve into texture.

## Expect a low hit rate

No two frames are the same. Shoot dozens, vary the speed and the length of the sweep, and expect to keep a handful. That unpredictability is part of the appeal.

> You are not recording the scene. You are painting with it.
lessons.challenge: Find a stand of trees with straight trunks. Shoot twenty frames at 1/4 s with vertical sweeps, varying the speed and length of the movement.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is a good starting shutter speed for ICM?
* Around 1/4 s to 1/2 s
- 1/1000 s
- 30 seconds

Q: Why do vertical sweeps suit tree trunks?
* Lines running with the movement stay as clean streaks
- Trees move in the wind
- Vertical movement freezes the leaves

Q: What hit rate should you expect?
* Low: shoot dozens, keep a handful
- Almost every frame will work
- Only the first frame will work

lessons.title: Architecture
lessons.summary: Buildings do not move and the light on them is predictable, which makes architecture the most patient subject there is. The hard part is the lines.
lessons.body:
A building is a composition someone has already designed. Your job is to find the angle and the light that show what the architect intended, or something they never saw.

One of my brothers is an architect, which probably explains why I notice the design of a building as much as the building itself.

## Commit to an angle

There are two strong ways to photograph a building, and one weak one.

- **Straight on:** stand square to the facade with the camera level, so every vertical stays vertical. Calm, graphic, exact.
- **Looking up:** point the camera steeply upwards and let the lines rush together. Dramatic and dizzying.
- **Half-way:** a slight upward tilt, where the walls lean just enough to look like a mistake. Avoid it.

[[photo:Speicherstadt balconies]]

Straight on and dead centre. Every line is parallel to the frame, so the repetition does all the work.

## Converging verticals

Tilt the camera up and parallel walls appear to lean in towards the top. Sometimes that is the point. When it is not, you can correct it.

[[guide:verticals]]

There are three ways to deal with it:

- Step back and use a longer lens, so you can keep the camera level
- Correct it in the edit with a perspective or upright tool, leaving room around the building because the correction crops the frame
- Use a tilt-shift lens, which moves the image up without tilting the camera

I sometimes straighten them in Lightroom with the Transform tool, but only when the photograph calls for it. If the lean is the point, I leave it alone.

## Light

**Blue hour** is the best time for buildings with lit windows. For about twenty minutes after sunset the sky and the interior lights are close in brightness, so both hold detail.

[[photo:Der Spiegel]]

**Side light** brings out texture in brick and stone. **Overcast** days suit detail and glass, with no hard reflections.

## Look up, look closer

The best architectural photographs are often not of the whole building. Stand in a courtyard or stairwell and look straight up. Fill the frame with a single repeating detail.

[[photo:Spiral]]

## Practical points

- Wide lenses stretch the edges of the frame. Keep important lines away from the corners
- Many buildings, shopping centres and stations do not allow tripods. Raise the ISO instead

- In cities I carry a light carbon-fibre Peak Design tripod. It is easier to carry all day and quicker to set up
- Private buildings and their courtyards may need permission to photograph

> Either keep the lines straight or make it obvious you meant them to lean.
lessons.challenge: Choose one building. Photograph it straight on with the camera level, then from close by looking steeply up. Avoid anything in between.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What causes converging verticals?
* Tilting the camera upwards
- Using a long shutter speed
- Shooting at blue hour

Q: Which is one way to keep verticals straight without editing?
* Step back and use a longer lens, keeping the camera level
- Use a wider lens and tilt up further
- Use a higher ISO

Q: Why leave room around a building if you plan to correct the verticals?
* The correction crops the edges of the frame
- It makes the file smaller
- It keeps the sky blue

lessons.title: Street
lessons.summary: Candid moments of everyday life in public places. Be ready before the moment arrives, and treat the people in your pictures with respect.
lessons.body:
Street photography captures ordinary life as it happens: people, gestures, light and coincidence in public places. The best moments last a fraction of a second, so the whole craft is about being ready before they arrive.

[[guide:zone]]

## Zone focusing

Autofocus can be too slow, or lock on the wrong thing. Instead, set the focus manually to a distance and an aperture that give a wide band of sharpness, then forget about it. At 35 mm and f/8, focus at 3 m and everything from about 1.9 m to 7 m is sharp. Anyone who steps into that zone is in focus the moment you press the shutter.

## Small and quiet

A small camera with a fixed 28 mm or 35 mm lens draws far less attention than a big zoom. Set a fast enough shutter to freeze people walking, around 1/250 s or faster, and let auto ISO cope with the light.

This is where a small camera earns its place. Mine is a Leica D-Lux 8. It is truly pocket-sized and its monochrome mode is brilliant, which makes it ideal for street.

## Find the scene, then wait

Rather than chasing people, find a good background: strong light and shadow, a striking wall, a doorway, a reflection. Then wait for someone to walk into it. This is sometimes called fishing, and it produces far stronger pictures than snapping at random.

## What to look for

- Gesture and expression, the split second that tells a story
- Light: low sun, hard shadows, shafts of light between buildings
- Layers: something near, something in the middle, something far
- Juxtaposition: two things in the frame that comment on each other

[[photo:xiangqi]]

Gesture. A hand reaching for a piece, the other player waiting. The background is soft enough to leave the two men and the board as the whole story.

[[photo:hydrant]]

Juxtaposition. The hydrant and the seated man have the same pale top and dark body, and the same downward tilt. Neither would be a photograph on its own.

[[photo:chinatown]]

Layers. Someone close, a family in the middle, a crowd beyond, all on one pavement.

## Respect

In the UK it is generally legal to photograph people in public places, but legal is not the same as right. Be open about what you are doing, smile, and if someone objects, delete the picture and move on. Take extra care with children and people in vulnerable situations. If you plan to use a picture commercially, you may need the person's written permission.

> Be ready before the moment, not after it.
lessons.challenge: Find a good background with strong light. Set up zone focus, stay in one spot for twenty minutes and photograph whoever walks into the scene.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is zone focusing?
* Presetting focus and aperture so a band of distance is already sharp
- Letting autofocus track a moving person
- Focusing on the background only

Q: Roughly what shutter speed freezes people walking?
* 1/250 s or faster
- 1/15 s
- 2 seconds

Q: What is "fishing" in street photography?
* Finding a good scene and waiting for someone to walk into it
- Following people until they do something interesting
- Shooting from the hip without looking

lessons.title: Woodland
lessons.summary: A wood is the hardest landscape to photograph well. The trick is finding order in the chaos, and the right weather does half of it for you.
lessons.body:
Walk into a wood with a camera and everything looks beautiful. Look at the pictures later and most of them are a tangle of trunks and branches with nowhere for the eye to rest. Woodland photography is mostly about simplifying.

[[guide:mist]]

## Wait for the right conditions

**Mist and fog** are the woodland photographer's best friends. Each row of trees fades a little more than the one in front, which separates the layers and gives the picture depth. Still autumn and spring mornings after a clear, cold night are the most likely times.

**Overcast days** come next. Soft light means no harsh patches of sun and deep shadow, and colours look richer. Bright sunshine through a canopy is the hardest light of all: the camera cannot hold the bright spots and the shadows at once.

**After rain** the bark darkens, moss glows and colours saturate. A polarising filter cuts the glare off wet leaves and makes the difference obvious.

## Find a subject

A wood needs a focal point as much as any landscape. Look for one tree that stands apart: a different shape, a different colour, a trunk catching the light. A path or a burn can lead the eye through.

## Use a longer lens

A wide lens takes in everything, and in a wood everything is the problem. A short telephoto, somewhere around 70 to 200 mm, lets you pick out a small, tidy scene from the mess and compresses the trunks into a pattern.

## Practical points

- Keep the camera level so trunks stay vertical and do not lean in
- Keep bright patches of sky out of the top of the frame
- Bring a tripod: woods are dark, even at midday
- Bluebell woods peak in late April and May; autumn colour usually peaks in late October

> Look for one tree, not the whole wood.
lessons.challenge: Go into a wood on an overcast day with a longer lens. Make five photographs, each built around a single tree.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does mist help woodland photographs?
* Each row of trees fades more, separating the layers
- It makes the colours brighter
- It allows faster shutter speeds

Q: What is the hardest light in a wood?
* Bright sun breaking through the canopy
- Soft overcast light
- Mist on a still morning

Q: Why use a longer lens in a wood?
* To pick out a small, tidy scene from the clutter
- To fit more of the wood in
- To make the trunks lean

lessons.title: Macro
lessons.summary: Close enough that a drop of dew becomes a landscape. Depth of field shrinks to millimetres, so focus and stillness become everything.
lessons.body:
True macro means reproducing the subject at life size or larger on the sensor, a ratio of 1:1. A 10 mm beetle covers 10 mm of sensor. At that scale, the ordinary rules of focus and light stop applying in the way you are used to.

[[guide:focus]]

## The depth of field problem

At life size, depth of field is tiny. On a full-frame camera at f/8 only about a millimetre of the subject is sharp. At f/2.8 it is about a third of a millimetre, barely the thickness of a petal.

Closing the aperture helps, but only up to a point. Beyond about f/16 diffraction starts to soften the whole image. f/8 to f/11 is the usual compromise.

## Focusing

- Set the focus manually and move the camera, not the focus ring
- Line the sensor up parallel with the most important plane of the subject, such as a wing or the face of a flower
- On an insect, the eyes must be sharp. Nothing else matters as much

## Focus stacking

Take a series of frames, each focused a little further into the subject, then blend them in software so the whole thing is sharp. It needs a still subject, a tripod and no wind. Many modern cameras can shoot the series for you.

## Equipment

A dedicated macro lens of 90 to 105 mm gives 1:1 and a comfortable working distance, so you do not scare insects or shade the subject. Close-up filters and extension tubes are cheaper ways to get close with lenses you already own.

## When to go

Early morning is best. The air is still, dew is on everything, and insects are cold and slow until the sun warms them up.

> At this scale, a breath of wind is an earthquake.
lessons.challenge: Go out early on a still morning. Find one small subject and take a series of frames, each focused a little further in, then try stacking them.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What does a 1:1 reproduction ratio mean?
* The subject appears life size on the sensor
- The subject fills the whole frame
- The lens is 100 mm long

Q: Why not just use f/22 for more depth of field?
* Diffraction softens the whole image
- f/22 lets in too much light
- Macro lenses do not go that far

Q: On an insect, what must be sharp?
* The eyes
- The legs
- The background

lessons.title: Abstract
lessons.summary: Take away the context and a photograph stops being of something. It becomes shape, line, colour and texture. Composition matters more, not less.
lessons.body:
An abstract photograph does not ask the viewer to recognise what it shows. It works on shape, line, colour, tone and texture alone. The subject can be anything: peeling paint, sand ripples, a reflection, the corner of a building.

[[guide:crop]]

## Get closer

The easiest way into abstraction is to remove context. Move in or zoom in until the frame holds only part of the subject. A whole boat is a boat. A curve of its hull against a stripe of water is a composition.

[[photo:angel]]

A famous sculpture, cropped until it is mostly line and tone. Without the whole figure, the ribs and the diagonal of the wing become the subject.

## Look for the elements

- **Line:** cracks, edges, cables, the boundary between two colours
- **Shape:** repeated forms, a single strong silhouette
- **Colour:** two colours side by side, or one colour in many shades
- **Texture:** rust, bark, stone, frost, best shown by light raking across from the side
- **Tone:** blocks of light and dark, especially in black and white

## The rules still apply

Without a recognisable subject, balance, contrast and placement carry the whole image. Thirds, leading lines and negative space all still work. A weak abstract is usually just a weak composition with nothing to hide behind.

## Ways to make one

- Shoot reflections in water, glass or polished metal
- Use a very shallow depth of field so most of the frame is soft colour
- Move the camera during the exposure (see the lesson on ICM)
- Turn the camera so the viewer cannot tell which way is up

## Titles

A title can open an abstract up or close it down. "Untitled" leaves it entirely to the viewer. Naming what it is can spoil the puzzle. Choose deliberately.

> Stop asking what it is. Ask whether it works.
lessons.challenge: Spend an hour photographing one ordinary object, such as a bike, a wall or a boat, without ever showing the whole thing.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is the easiest way into abstraction?
* Remove context by moving or zooming in
- Use a wider lens
- Add more elements to the frame

Q: Which light best shows texture?
* Light raking across from the side
- Flat light from behind the camera
- Light from directly overhead at noon

Q: Do composition rules apply to abstract photographs?
* Yes, more than ever
- No, anything goes
- Only the rule of thirds

lessons.title: Behind the shot: Deadvlei
lessons.summary: Flooded roads, a barefoot wade and a quiet spell before the crowds. One photograph and how it was made.
lessons.body:
[[shot:first-light]]

## Why I was there

We were in Namibia on a photography holiday with the brilliant James Kerwin. Most of the trip was urbex: abandoned villages slowly being reclaimed by the sand. Deadvlei was the big landscape stop.

## Getting there

Saying it was easy would be a lie. Heavy rain had flooded the roads, and parts of them were close to impassable. Somehow the four-by-fours pushed through rivers of muddy water, and we got there just as the sun was about to come up over the dunes.

We parked, took off our shoes and socks, and waded across more flooded ground, the wet sand shifting under our feet, to reach the trees. Then we set up and started shooting.

## The moment

We had a good stretch of time before the sun cleared the dunes. It was the best part of the morning: the light was still workable, the trees threw long shadows across the pan, and the crowds hadn't arrived yet.

Once the sun was fully up, the light turned very bright and the best of it was gone.

## How I shot it

The pan itself was dry: just crusty, sun-baked ground, despite all the water we had waded through to get there.

This was taken in that early window. The first sun is catching the tree, while the dune behind it is still in shadow.

I shot it on the tripod at 400 mm. The honest reason for the long lens was practical. Standing well back meant I didn't have to walk into the scene and end up in someone else's photograph. With a group of photographers all working the same trees, that matters.

It also changes the picture. From that far back, the dune stops looking like a dune and becomes a plain dark backdrop that fills the frame behind the tree. The Telephoto landscapes lesson explains why.

The settings were f/10 at 1/100 s. With the tree and the dune both so far from the camera, f/10 was enough to keep everything sharp.

## In the edit

I can't remember exactly what I did to this one. Whatever it was, it will have been light. That's how I edit everything: Lightroom and a few small adjustments, nothing that changes what was there.
lessons.challenge: Next time you are somewhere busy, resist walking in closer. Step back, use a longer lens, and see what it does to the picture.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why was this photograph taken at 400 mm?
* To stand back without walking into other people's photographs
- To fit more of the pan into the frame
- Because it lets in more light

Q: When was the best light that morning?
* Before the sun cleared the dunes
- Once the sun was fully up
- At midday

Q: Why was f/10 enough to keep the tree and the dune sharp?
* Everything in the frame was a long way from the camera
- The tripod adds depth of field
- f/10 always gives the most depth of field
